title: Five concepts, not fifty
spec: M07 · what deserves a file, and what is already free
intro: Turn orderflow into an OKF bundle. The hard part is not the Markdown — it is saying no. A concept that restates a function signature costs real maintenance and buys nothing the AST did not already give you.

provenance.source: a replayed authoring session over labs/sample-project, targeting the bundle described in labs/M07-orderflow-bundle/README.md. The citations, contracts and decisions quoted are read from the real files in labs/sample-project/docs/; steps 4 and 5 carry their own citations.

foot: Build the whole bundle in labs/M07-orderflow-bundle/ — five concepts, an index, and bidirectional links.

steps.title: Inventory the repo, then say no a lot
narrative: orderflow has fifteen files, three services, thirty-six symbols and three documents. The naive move is one concept per file, and it is wrong. The right question for every candidate is a single test: could a parser have told me this?

If the answer is yes, the structural graph from Track 2 already knows it, for free, deterministically, and — crucially — it will still be right after the next refactor. A concept file that duplicates it is a second copy of one fact, maintained by hand, guaranteed to drift.

Curated narrative knowledge is the residue: the things that are true about this system and written nowhere in it. Contracts between services. Decisions and their consequences. Policy baked into a constant. Run the test down the list.
steps.youDo: ls -R labs/sample-project, then for each candidate ask: is this derivable from the AST? If yes, it is not a concept.

steps.title: A concept that earns its file
narrative: Here is billing-service.md. Read it once as a human, then read it again asking which sentences a parser could have produced. The answer is: almost none of them.

That the event bus is synchronous and in-process is in the code. That it was chosen over a broker, that events are lost on crash, and that going multi-process means replacing it and updating the payment.settled contract — that is ADR-001, and no AST will ever recover it. That shared/auth.py reads the signing key at import time, so a key rotation requires a rolling restart of billing — that is the runbook, and it is the difference between a safe deploy and an outage.

Notice the shape as much as the content: Responsibilities, then Dependencies, then Citations, in that order, in every Service concept. Consistency of body structure matters more to an agent than any individual field, because fifty identically-shaped files can be parsed mechanically and fifty differently-shaped ones become fifty interpretation problems.

steps.title: A concept that wastes its file
narrative: Now the one that looks productive and is not. Someone works down invoice.py writing a concept per function, and produces this.

Every sentence in it is already in the repository twice — once in the source and once in the graph — and the graph's copy is better: it is complete, it carries provenance, and it updates when the code does. This copy is prose, it is unversioned against the function it describes, and it is silently wrong the moment somebody renames the parameter.
Toggle the panes. Same fact, two costs. The bundle version costs an author, a reviewer, and an ongoing maintenance obligation nobody scheduled. The graph version costs one query.
steps.youDo: Try the test on your own draft bundle: for each concept, delete it and ask whether an agent with the structural graph would notice. If the answer is no, it was never knowledge.

before.title: THE WASTEFUL CONCEPT — hand-written, will rot

lines: Marks an invoice as paid. Takes an `invoice_id` string and returns the
invoice as a dict. Raises `KeyError` if the invoice is unknown.

views.text: Author cost: ten minutes. Review cost: someone must check it against the source. Maintenance cost: forever, and nothing will tell you when it stops being true. Rename invoice_id and this file lies with a straight face, having passed every lint rule in the bundle.

Author cost: zero. Maintenance cost: zero — it is regenerated from the syntax tree. And it answers a question the concept file never could: who calls this, completely, with the provenance label saying the edge was read off the AST rather than guessed.

steps.title: index.md — the file the agent reads before touching the repo
narrative: The index is not a table of contents for humans. It is the pre-flight read: title and one-line description per concept, pulled straight from frontmatter, and nothing else. An agent reads it, decides which one concept the task needs, and loads that.

Here is the arithmetic on orderflow, measured rather than asserted. The whole of services/ and shared/ is 9,798 characters across fourteen Python files — call it 2,450 tokens to read the codebase cold. The M06 concept files measure 876 and 920 characters, so a real concept costs about 220 tokens. Index plus one concept lands near 400.

Be honest about what that ratio proves: about six-to-one on a fifteen-file toy, which is not a business case. What matters is the slope. The source side grows with every file you add; the index grows by one line per concept and the agent still loads exactly one. On a thousand-file repo that is the difference between working and overflowing.
steps.youDo: Count it yourself: wc -c labs/sample-project/services/*/*.py labs/sample-project/shared/*.py against wc -c knowledge/index.md knowledge/services/billing-service.md. Record both — the capstone reuses them.

before.title: TWO WAYS TO LEARN THE SAME TERRITORY

items.label: read the source
items.note: 9,798 characters across 14 .py files in services/ and shared/ — measured

items.label: index + 1 concept
items.note: ~180 for the index, ~220 for one concept — concept sizes measured from the M06 solution files

view.text: Six-to-one on fifteen files is a teaching number, not a saving — the same ~500-file floor that undercuts every tool in M05 applies to bundles too. The claim worth defending is different and stronger: the pre-flight cost is bounded by the task, not by the repo. Add nine hundred more files and the agent still reads one index line and one concept. That is why an index bloated with detail is a real bug: it re-couples the read to the size of the bundle.

steps.title: Lint it — then check the direction nobody checks
narrative: Five concepts, zero errors. That is the gate from M06 doing exactly its job, and it is worth being clear about what it proved: the bundle is well-formed. It did not prove the bundle is complete.

Here is the gap. billing-service.md says it publishes payment.settled and links to notifications. Does notifications-service.md link back? Nothing in the spec requires it, no lint rule you have written checks it, and an agent that loads only the notifications concept will never learn that billing depends on it. One-directional links are how bundles silently rot.
Fix it, then run the harder check: rename a linked file without updating its inbound links and confirm your dangling-link rule fails. If it passes, you have built a linter that agrees with you.

before.title: WHAT THE BUNDLE CLAIMS vs WHAT THE AST KNOWS

widest blast radius in the repo; notifications never touches it

view.text: The AST is right about structure; the bundle is right about why — and the disagreement itself is a maintenance signal, not an error in either. Use the links for orientation and intent; use the verified edges for impact analysis you are going to bet a refactor on. A bundle that is asked to do the second job will confidently tell an agent that billing has two dependencies on the sprint somebody added a third.
